Senses.Explanation: Linji uses carrying oil without spilling as the image of meticulous observance, then denies that such care settles the matter when the eye of the Way is unclear. In the same address he ranges from fasting and keeping precepts through solitary lodging, one meal before noon, long sitting, and six periods of observance. The preserved copies agree that even flawless oil-carrying leaves one owing the donors when the eye of the Way is unclear.

Senses.Explanation: The jackal's cry is a Chan verdict on speech that lacks the standing of a lion's roar. Masters apply it to asserted attainment, derivative formulations, and teachers wearing a lion's skin while producing a jackal's sound. Baizhang Huaihai calls the claim that present awareness is one's own buddha language resembling a jackal's cry. Linji Yixuan rebukes one who wears a lion's skin but makes that cry. Dahui Zonggao repeats the inherited contrast between gain-seeking speech and the lion's roar, then applies the animal image to teachers who reject awakening. Luoshan Daoxian makes the two voices relational in an encounter: either participant may cry like the jackal or roar like the lion according to the living exchange.

Senses.Explanation: The wild fox is anchored by Baizhang’s fox case, while separate uses name an actual fox or denounce a person as fox-like; the three referents remain distinct. A fox story becomes a named public case: the story's unnamed former abbot says that answering 'does not fall under cause and effect' brought five hundred fox births, while Baizhang Huaihai answers 'is not blind to cause and effect.' Zhenjing Kewen heads a verse simply 'Wild Fox'; Xiaoyin Daxin repeatedly raises 'Baizhang's wild-fox story' in the chamber to question monks, and Shita Xuanmi raises the same longer title in a hall address. The abbreviated case-name is a textual object, not the animal in the story and not a person denounced as a fox.

Senses.Note: Baizhang Huaihai supplies the corpse and cremation; Fachang Yu and Hongfu Ziwen supply falling-into and escaping-from predicates; Dahui Zonggao supplies the five-hundred-birth fox. The source presents the former abbot without a personal name, so the entry invents no synthetic master identity.

Senses.Explanation: Speakers use ‘wild-fox Chan’ as an adverse label for Chan they present as counterfeit, distorted, or merely clever. The phrase can allude to the Baizhang fox case, but its attested use also ranges beyond that case as a charge against other people’s teaching or performance. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that Liao'an Qingyu, Ruibai Mingxue, Fangrong Tongxi, or another named speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after an unnamed monk shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).

Senses.Explanation: Linji’s “wild-fox sprites” (野狐精魅) names the deceiving creatures that, in his address, fasten upon respectable men and women. The complete passage first describes shaven men who see spirits, point east and west, and pronounce upon fine or rainy weather. Linji then says that good households are seized by these wild-fox sprites, after which they manufacture marvels and demand food money. Six retained records transmit this same governed Linji passage with minor graphic differences; they are recension evidence for one address, not six independent inventions of the label.
